extracted.intended_audience: newspaper reporters, city editors, and journalism students
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidelines for producing follow-up (folo) stories and short "color" feature items for newspapers, including types of follow-ups, structural requirements, narrative techniques, subject-selection rules, sourcing, and editorial/edition precautions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Folo — entirely new aspect
rubrics_metrics.description: A follow-up that supplies an entirely new aspect so the story remains alive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: first-day relation announced Patton & Morse factory added 200 employees; a folo learns the company received a government order assuring six months' full-time operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Folo — consequence/result of original action
rubrics_metrics.description: A folo that reports the consequence or result of the original action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: original: 'Three persons injured in collision.' Folo next day: one of the injured has died.

rubrics_metrics.name: Folo — relation to previous events
rubrics_metrics.description: A folo that places the incident in relation to prior events or patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: explain that an accident was the fourth traffic fatality this year on the same road.

rubrics_metrics.name: Folo — reaction to the first story
rubrics_metrics.description: A folo that records reactions, giving versions or views not presented in the first story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: first account described employees threatening to strike; folo presents management's version via interviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Folo — local ends to out-of-town stories
rubrics_metrics.description: A folo that localizes an out-of-town event by asking whether the same could/does happen locally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: distant hospital patient died when lights went out; local folo asks officials whether that could happen locally and why not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Folo — same story with more details
rubrics_metrics.description: A folo that expands the original by adding more details and human-interest specifics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: original four-inch account of rescued canoeists expanded with how they felt during the night and their physical suffering to make interesting reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Folo — same story from a different angle
rubrics_metrics.description: A folo that retells the same action from a new angle, possibly as a color story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: first-day straight news about an engineer braking for a dog; folo may present action from the dog's point of view or as a color piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Folo — installment story (serializing exclusive details)
rubrics_metrics.description: Splitting an exclusive into multiple days to get multiple scoops, used only when the information is exclusive and will remain so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: learn exclusively of a 50-room hotel addition and publish initial announcement then later detail; do this only if exclusivity is certain and will hold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tie-in with yesterday (folo lead/linkage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every folo must include a tie-in to the original story so readers who missed the first account understand the follow-up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tie-in should present essential facts; if brief, work into the lead; if long, run as second paragraph. As story remains alive longer, tie-in can be shortened.

rubrics_metrics.name: Folo sourcing — diversify and avoid single-source repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: When a story stays alive, find more than one source to avoid quoting the same person repeatedly and to produce more complete coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple sources produce fuller stories; relying repeatedly on one person is monotonous and incomplete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Masking sources sparingly ('a well informed source')
rubrics_metrics.description: Conceal specific source identity when necessary, but reserve generic attribution for genuinely large stories and use it cautiously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: City editors dislike overuse. Masking may prevent rivals from locating the source but cannot be relied upon; overuse encourages guessing and substitutes imagination for fact-gathering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Edition protection for exclusives
rubrics_metrics.description: Protect exclusives by controlling which edition they appear in and notifying make-up staff to avoid early exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: mark scoops 'City Edition Only.' Failure to protect can let rivals steal the story from an early edition. Also, restoring stories removed earlier is necessary to avoid later scooping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline must match color story content
rubrics_metrics.description: Color story headlines unmistakably signal the piece's nature; a mismatch between headline promise and story quality causes reader resentment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the headline lures readers expecting an emotionally different item and the story is weak, readers will feel deceived and resentful; ensure headline accurately reflects what the story delivers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every word must contribute (color procedure)
rubrics_metrics.description: In color stories, every word should contribute to the effect or impact the reporter wants to make.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Color stories rely on emotional appeal; words are slivers compared to lead-story news, so trim everything that doesn't add to the intended impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understatement over overstatement (color procedure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Understatement is usually more effective than overstatement in color writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't force emotion; leave readers room to 'complete' the effect. Overplaying emotions causes resistance; subtlety often leaves readers wanting a little more and thus more affected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use fiction devices (transferable techniques)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use devices from short fiction to obtain effects in color writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short-story methods (small cast, scene construction, mood control, episodic structure, dialog, etc.) can be adapted wholesale to newspaper color pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color stories must be high quality; use sparingly
rubrics_metrics.description: A color story is 'a hundred per cent, or it is zero' — do color infrequently so each item is strong; quality counts far more than quantity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If too many weak color pieces appear, a reporter's reputation suffers. Occasional crackerjack color items build a stronger reputation than many mediocre ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative device — keep the cast small
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit the cast of characters to one person or a small group to avoid confusing readers in short pieces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short color stories (often under 300 words) don't allow readers time to learn many characters; omit minor figures and present only the essential central actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative device — use jerky/impressionistic (staccato) style
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ a brisk, impressionistic style (staccato sentences) to indicate action and movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quick movement keeps attention. If a color story 'limps', trim it to two-thirds or half its original space to intensify action by removing minor details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative device — subordinate everything to one mood
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure the story evokes a single mood; do not mix conflicting emotions in a short piece.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If aiming to provoke laughter, avoid mournful elements; mixing emotions in brief pieces usually kills the effect — only long pieces can shift emotions credibly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative device — split into episodes and avoid flashbacks
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure the story into a few tight episodes (like acts) and avoid flashbacks or secondary actions that diffuse impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give each element completely when it appears (identify people fully on first mention). Too many episodes or scene changes in a short story risk confusing readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify subject matter (appropriateness check)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether an incident is a proper subject for color writing; not every event can be turned into color.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid: (a) trifling happenings with no engaging aspect; (b) deceiving pathos — 'almost' pathos; (c) incidents that begin humorous but end in real sorrow or risk (do not treat truly harmful outcomes lightly); (d) invasions of family privacy unless handled expertly. If subject isn't appropriate, either drop color or use straight news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word choice and diction — immediate comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: Use immediate, easily comprehensible language; avoid recondite words and misfitting phrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex or obscure words (e.g., 'ternary') force readers to translate and lose the story's dramatic quality. One wrong word (e.g., 'chirps' vs 'roar') can destroy an impression. Avoid excessive alliteration — a little is emphatic, too much is forced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural necessity — subject must be an incident/action
rubrics_metrics.description: The compact color story must be about an incident or happening — action is essential; pure description without action is unsatisfying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descriptive passages without action (e.g., a sunset) are difficult to sustain in short color pieces; action drives reader engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural necessity — incident should contain conversation/dialog
rubrics_metrics.description: Include dialog because quoted speech makes a story more lifelike and breaks text into short, readable paragraphs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even animal stories can often offer dialog; dialog also improves optical readability versus long grey blocks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural necessity — episode must have a central character
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be one central figure more prominent than others throughout the piece.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shifting prominence mid-story (first one person, then another) ruins clarity; rewrite to keep one character dominant to preserve focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural necessity — episode must be true (no invented details)
rubrics_metrics.description: All elements must be true; inventing details to strengthen a weak incident is unacceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fabrication brands the newspaper a liar and becomes habitual; initial small inventions lead to larger omissions of reporting and eventual staff consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good reporting is necessary for color
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to do color on demand depends on thorough reporting, keen observation, and cultivated local contacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Color items are by-products of good reporting; reporters must keep eyes and ears open, know many people (newsstand clerks, hotel staff, station workers) who can tip them to tidbits; places where people congregate (stations, lobbies, elevators, buses) are fertile ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rescuing weak color by small edits / trimming
rubrics_metrics.description: Many failing color stories can be rescued by deleting misfit words, trimming nonessentials, or tightening structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trim corns and parings, delete secondary detail, remove awkward or grandiose phrases; reducing length often intensifies action and makes the story twice as powerful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish color, human interest, and feature
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand the difference: a color story is a short feature emphasizing 'the way it's written'; features are seminews and more evergreen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A feature can run days later and spend space explaining background (e.g., how a fire alarm system works), whereas color is short, episodic, and immediate; terminology varies by office but the functional distinctions matter for timing and approach.
